title: Deer antlers re-form an ectopic branch at a past injury site year after year

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Deer antlers re-form an ectopic branch at a past injury site year after year

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In deer trophic memory, an ectopic branch is formed in the otherwise stereotyped antler at the location of earlier damage year after year, long after the damaged rack has been shed, a memory of 3D position held by scalp cells that regenerate the antler annually.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Levin M 2023, Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind › Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Memory and target morphology

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Trophic memory in deer (Bubenik and Pavlansky 1965; Lobo et al. 2014) enables an ectopic branch in their otherwise stereotypical antler structure to be formed year after year, at a specific point of earlier damage, long after the damaged antler rack has been shed

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Levin M, “Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind”, Animal cognition (2023), doi:10.1007/s10071-023-01780-3; section “Basal cognition without neurons: what dynamic bodies think about › Memory and target morphology”. Scope: Deer (Cervidae) antler regeneration

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2023-glue-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.54

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Spatial recurrence over annual replacement is measurable from serial morphology. Available public collections are unlikely to pair repeated individuals with documented injuries, and recurrence alone does not identify a stored positional memory.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Register photographs or scans of antlers across years to the scalp, map prior injury location, and test whether an ectopic branch recurs at that location more than expected from normal branching variation. Uninjured matched animals and contralateral antlers provide controls.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Local persistent scarring or niche alteration rivals a memory interpretation.

Historical longitudinal photographs and injury coordinates may not be public.

Antler branch variation is naturally high.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.62
data existence: 0.32

discriminating power: 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Injury site and later branch position are measurable, but no open dataset of antler injuries and subsequent morphology exists to analyze. The published cases are narrative observations. Distinguishing a remembered target from a persistent local scar would require new paired records, or at least a compiled individual-level series that is not currently public.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Record the position of an experimental or accidental injury on a deer antler and the position of any extra branch in subsequent years after the rack is shed. Coincidence of the ectopic branch with the old injury site across years would support the positional memory; failure of the site to recur, or recurrence explained by a permanent pedicle scar visible in the scalp, would count against a memory held only as information about past damage.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A structural scar in the pedicle can place the next branch without a stored 3D memory.

The reports are small historical case series, not a public table of injury coordinates and later racks.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.25
analysis feasibility: 0.3
data adequacy: 0.2
